title: Big Tech H-1B Filings Plummet as Layoffs and Fee Hikes Squeeze Indian Workers
excerpt: Google and Meta saw visa applications drop by nearly half in early 2026, while rolling layoffs froze green card sponsorships for thousands of Indian tech professionals caught in a tightening immigration pipeline.
body:
• H-1B visa filings by Amazon, Google, Meta, Apple, and Microsoft fell sharply in Q1 2026, with Google and Meta applications dropping by nearly half year-over-year.
  • Google has restarted its PERM green card sponsorship program in 2026 after a three-year freeze triggered by 12,000 layoffs in January 2023, but strict eligibility criteria exclude remote workers and low performers.
  • The Trump administration's $100,000 H-1B petition fee—ruled unlawful by a federal judge in June 2026—and the DOL's 180-day layoff rule have compounded delays for Indian workers, who hold 71% of all approved H-1B visas.
  • Nvidia bucked the trend as the only major tech firm to increase H-1B filings, rising from 369 to 434 year-over-year.

The Numbers Tell the Story

Federal labor filing data for the first quarter of fiscal year 2026 (October–December 2025) reveals a severe contraction in H-1B sponsorship across Silicon Valley's largest employers. Amazon, the biggest filer among tech giants, saw certified applications fall to 3,057 from 4,647 in the same period a year earlier. Google and Meta's filings dropped by approximately 50%, according to a Business Insider analysis of Department of Labor records. Apple, Microsoft, IBM, Salesforce, and Tesla all reported declines.

The lone outlier: Nvidia. The chipmaker increased its certified H-1B applications from 369 to 434, a modest but symbolic rise. CEO Jensen Huang said the company would continue hiring immigrants despite the fee increase, citing the specialized nature of AI and chip design talent.

What's Driving the Decline

Two forces converged to create the downturn. First, the Trump administration's immigration policy overhaul, introduced in September 2025, imposed a $100,000 surcharge on new H-1B petitions—a move designed to shift hiring toward domestic workers. The fee drew immediate legal challenges, and on June 8, 2026, a federal judge struck it down as unlawful. But its months-long enforcement had already chilled filing activity across the sector.

Second, rolling layoffs gutted headcount at every major tech firm. Amazon cut 16,000 corporate jobs in January 2026, following 14,000 reductions in October 2025. Meta laid off hundreds in March. Google, which slashed 12,000 workers in January 2023, conducted additional cuts in subsequent rounds. Each layoff wave triggered Department of Labor regulations that effectively froze green card sponsorship for months.

The 180-Day Trap

Under federal regulation 20 CFR § 656.17(k), any employer that conducts a layoff must take additional steps before filing a PERM labor certification—the first stage of employer-sponsored green card processing. Companies must identify all "potentially qualified" laid-off U.S. workers in similar roles, notify them of the open position, and consider them in good faith. Failure to comply triggers audits or outright denial.

For companies with continuous layoff cycles, the 180-day window never closes. "People's hands are tied for six months. And this is after the last layoff," Xiao Wang, co-founder and CEO of Boundless Immigration, told Bloomberg Law. "There are companies that have had multiple rounds of layoffs, so the process will keep getting pushed back."

"People think it's the end of their immigrant dreams and it's not. With some creative management, companies can work through this just fine."

— Davis Bae, Co-Chair of Immigration Practice, Fisher & Phillips LLP

Immigration law firm Badmus & Associates noted that the "Google approach"—pausing PERM filings entirely to wait out the regulatory window—has become the standard playbook for large employers. The firm warned that remote work adds another layer of risk: if a PERM position is listed as fully remote, the DOL may treat the entire United States as the relevant labor market, meaning any layoff of a U.S. worker in a similar role anywhere in the country could trigger notification requirements.

Google's Restart—With Strings Attached

After three years on ice, Google announced in late 2025 that it would resume PERM green card sponsorships in 2026. The company told staff that eligible employees would be contacted by external immigration counsel in Q1 2026 to begin the process.

But the restart comes with significant guardrails. Employees must hold a relevant degree and work experience, maintain at least a "Moderate Impact" performance rating, and be in an office-based role—fully remote workers are excluded unless they agree to relocate. Workers at Level 3 or below face long odds of qualifying. Google also advised employees against international travel during the process due to visa processing uncertainties.

The move signals renewed commitment to retaining foreign talent, but the strict criteria mean many H-1B holders at the company will remain in limbo, particularly those in lower-level roles or distributed teams.

What It Means for Indian Tech Workers

India accounts for 71% of all approved H-1B visa beneficiaries, making Indian nationals the demographic most exposed to these shifts. The squeeze is multi-layered: reduced filings shrink the number of new visa slots, layoff-driven PERM freezes delay green card processing for those already in the U.S., and country-specific green card backlogs mean Indian applicants already face wait times stretching decades.

For H-1B holders who were laid off, the clock is especially unforgiving. They typically have a 60-day grace period to find a new employer willing to sponsor an H-1B transfer—a compressed timeline in a market where tech hiring has slowed considerably. Immigration attorneys recommend exploring alternatives including the National Interest Waiver and O-1 Extraordinary Ability visa, which bypass the PERM requirement entirely.

U.S. lawmakers have also entered the fray. Senators Chuck Grassley and Dick Durbin sent letters to Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Apple, Walmart, Cognizant, and Tata Consultancy Services demanding data on H-1B hires, wages, and potential displacement of American workers. "With all of the homegrown American talent relegated to the sidelines, we find it hard to believe that Amazon cannot find qualified American tech workers," the senators wrote.

What's Next

The federal court ruling striking down the $100,000 fee could ease some pressure on future filing cycles, though the government may appeal. Meanwhile, DOL audit rates for tech company PERM applications are at record highs in 2026, and the agency is using automated cross-referencing tools to match filings against public layoff announcements and WARN Act notices.

For now, the landscape remains treacherous for visa-dependent workers. Google's restart is a positive signal, but the broader trend—fewer filings, more layoffs, and tighter scrutiny—suggests the pipeline from H-1B to permanent residency will remain constrained well into 2027.
